goust.story: Goust is a hamlet of 2.5 square kilometres on a plateau in the Pyrenees mountains of France, reached by a footpath across a bridge called the Pont d'Enfer. It belongs to Laruns, a French commune (local municipality). Writers in the 19th century described Goust as an independent republic. The idea goes back to an 1827 description by Joseph Lainé. In 1858 another writer, Samazeuilh, said Lainé had been speaking in metaphor and that later authors had taken him literally. Residents paid their taxes to the government in Laruns and went to the church there for baptisms, weddings and burials. American newspapers reported an uprising in 1896 over a ban on newspapers, but that report has never been verified. Goust's independence is treated today as folklore, and the hamlet is an ordinary part of France.
goust.mechanism: Being described as independent does not make a place independent. Goust's residents went on paying tax to French local government, which shows the state was in charge throughout.
goust.laws: French law, with residents paying taxes in Laruns
goust.recognition: None, because the independence is folklore

holy-empire-of-reunion.story: The Holy Empire of Reunion is an invented country created on 28 August 1997 by law students at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro in Brazil. It claims Réunion, an island of about 2,511 square kilometres in the Indian Ocean that is an overseas department of France, meaning a full administrative part of the French state. The project has been described as a parody of the French department and as a simulation for practising politics and constitutional law. A Brazilian newspaper covered it in 1998 when it moved onto the internet. No report shows any attempt to take control of the island or any response from France, and none says whether the project is still active.
holy-empire-of-reunion.mechanism: A claim made from another country over land already governed by France has no legal effect. A student simulation of a state creates no rights over the place it names.

hutt-river.story: The Principality of Hutt River was a farm in Western Australia, 517 kilometres north of Perth, whose owner declared it an independent country. Leonard Casley, a wheat farmer, had about 4,000 hectares of crop ready to harvest when new government quotas allowed him to sell only about 40 hectares' worth. In protest, on 21 April 1970 he declared his 75-square-kilometre farm the independent Hutt River Province. He later said that a letter the government had not answered gave it self-rule in practice from 1972, and he began calling himself Prince Leonard. He issued a currency, stamps and passports, none of which any government accepted. Australia still expected him to pay tax. In February 1977 he was convicted for failing to give tax documents to the Australian Taxation Office, and that December he declared war on Australia, ending the war days later. The High Court of Australia dismissed one of his applications as fatuous, frivolous and vexatious, a phrase for a case with no legal merit. In June 2017 a judge of the Supreme Court of Western Australia rejected the argument that the court had no power over Hutt River and ordered Leonard to pay A$2.7 million and his son Arthur A$242,000 in unpaid tax. Leonard died in 2019. On 3 August 2020 another son, Graeme, dissolved the principality, citing hard times in the pandemic, and the farm went on sale.
hutt-river.mechanism: Declaring secession does not take a person outside national tax law. Australian courts ruled that Hutt River's owners owed tax like any other Australians.
hutt-river.stopped_by: The founder's son Graeme dissolved it in 2020, citing the pandemic
hutt-river.passports: Issued, but accepted by no government
hutt-river.laws: Royal titles for family members, and no court of its own is reported
hutt-river.challenge: Lost repeatedly, with a 1977 tax conviction, a dismissed High Court application and a 2017 tax judgment

islandia.story: The Principality of Islandia is a micronation, meaning a self-declared country that no government recognises, on Coffee Caye, a mangrove-covered island of about half a hectare in the Caribbean Sea, a short boat trip from Belize City. Gareth Johnson and Marshall Mayer founded it in February 2018. It was the first attempt at a micronation paid for by crowdfunding, in which many people each contribute money. It has about 250 citizens, none of whom live on the island, which can be rented for camping trips. A 2024 article reported plans to elect a new head of state. The island remains part of Belize.
islandia.mechanism: Buying an island gives ownership of the land. Belize keeps its power to govern it, so a group of owners calling themselves a country does not change whose law applies.
islandia.why: Position replaced with published coordinates for Coffee Caye (17°34'30"N 88°09'46"W). Founders are Gareth Johnson and Marshall Mayer (founder field says Not stated).

jamtland-republic.story: The Republic of Jämtland, in full the United Republics of Jämtland, Härjedalen and Ravund, is a humorous cultural and marketing project in the Jämtland region of Sweden. It began in 1963 and 1964 as a reaction to people moving away from the county and to a plan by the central government to merge Jämtland County with neighbouring Västernorrland. Its founders formed a Liberation Movement and gathered support through Storsjöyran, a local festival. Their argument looks back to the 10th to 12th centuries, when Jämtland governed itself and answered to no crown, until the Norwegian crown annexed it in 1178. Its presidents have been entertainers, starting with the television performer Yngve Gamlin in 1963 and, since 2022, the actress Eva Röse. The comedian Moltas Erikson, president from 1983 to 1988, called the movement 51 percent jest and 49 percent earnest. Local support for real independence is low, and the movement mainly works to preserve Jämtlandic culture and language. The area remains part of Sweden.
jamtland-republic.mechanism: A region can use a real history of self-rule to promote its culture without changing its legal status. Sweden's government and law continue to apply there.
jamtland-republic.why: Founding given as 1963-64 with its actual cause (emigration and a county merger plan); founder field Not stated could name the Liberation Movement and Yngve Gamlin.

kalakuta-republic.story: The Kalakuta Republic was the home compound of the Nigerian musician Fela Kuti at 14 Agege Motor Road, in the Mushin area of Lagos, Nigeria. After returning from the United States in 1970, Kuti declared the compound independent of the state, which was then run by the military. It housed his family and band, a recording studio and a free health clinic. On 18 February 1977 about a thousand armed soldiers attacked, and the compound burned to the ground. Kuti's mother, Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was thrown from a second-floor window and died after about eight weeks in a coma. The site was later rebuilt, in an effort led by Governor Babatunde Fashola, and it opened as the Kalakuta Republic Museum on 15 October 2012.
kalakuta-republic.mechanism: The Nigerian military government answered a symbolic claim of independence with force. No court ever considered the claim.

keraton-agung-sejagat.story: Keraton Agung Sejagat, meaning Universal Grand Throne, was a mystical movement and invented kingdom based in Purworejo Regency, Central Java, Indonesia. Its founders, Totok Santoso Hadiningrat and Dyah Gitarja, began it in 2018 and gathered around 450 members. Hadiningrat said that a ruler of the old Majapahit Empire had handed sovereignty, meaning supreme authority, to the Portuguese in 1518 on condition that it be returned after 500 years. On that basis he claimed authority over every country on Earth, including the United Nations and the Pentagon. Members paid about 200 dollars each for uniforms and titles. In January 2020 the group held a public ritual in a Purworejo township, and residents who were uneasy about it complained to the police. Police arrested the two founders days later. On 21 January Hadiningrat told a press conference that the kingdom was a scam and its history was made up. A University of Indonesia historian also pointed out that the Majapahit Empire had collapsed in 1478, before the supposed treaty. No report says how any case against them ended.
keraton-agung-sejagat.mechanism: Selling titles on the strength of an invented treaty is treated as a matter for the police. Indonesian police investigated the group as an ordinary local complaint, and the founder admitted the scam.
keraton-agung-sejagat.why: Founders named (Totok Santoso Hadiningrat, Dyah Gitarja); Purworejo base now confirmed by a retrieved page.

killington-new-hampshire.story: Killington is a town of 1,407 people (2020 census) in Vermont, in the northeastern United States, whose voters have twice approved the idea of leaving Vermont to join neighbouring New Hampshire. The first vote came at a town meeting in March 2004, by voice, with officials estimating that about two-thirds of the 200 to 300 people present were in favour. Residents were angry about Vermont's system for paying for schools, adopted in 1997 under a state Supreme Court order, which sharply raised property taxes in towns with valuable property such as Killington. They pointed out that the town was first chartered by New Hampshire in 1761, and it had spent about $20,000 studying the move. New Hampshire's governor, Craig Benson, said he did not think it would happen. The votes were largely symbolic, because the move would need approval from both state legislatures and the United States Congress. Killington remains a town in Vermont.
killington-new-hampshire.mechanism: Moving a town from one American state to another needs both state legislatures and Congress to agree, so a local vote alone changes nothing.

add_sources.t: Killington, Vt., Voters Choose to Secede (Fox News)

killington-new-hampshire.why: Added missing start year (March 2004 town meeting vote).

kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.story: The Kingdom of Araucania and Patagonia was a state proclaimed in 1860 by a French lawyer over the lands of the Mapuche, an Indigenous people, in what is now southern Chile and Argentina. Antoine de Tounens, a former lawyer from Perigueux, decided to go there after reading La Araucana, an epic poem about the region. He reached Chile in 1858 and met Mapuche leaders south of the Biobio River, promising guns and French help to keep them independent of Chile. Some leaders, including Kilapan and Kalfukura, backed him, possibly because they believed a European could help their cause. In November 1860 he issued two decrees saying that Araucania and eastern Patagonia belonged to no other state and naming himself King Orelie-Antoine I. He named Perquenco his capital, created a flag and had coins minted. Chile's president authorised his arrest, which came on 5 January 1862. A court in Santiago declared him insane that September, and in October he was expelled to France. He tried three more times to return, and each time he was captured and sent back. His declaration has been described as one cause of the Chilean occupation of Araucania, and his death has been attributed to ill health from his captivity.
kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.mechanism: A proclamation does not create a state when a neighbouring government can arrest the claimant and its courts can remove him. The land also already had its own people, the Mapuche, whose rights a foreign king's decree could not decide.
kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.stopped_by: Chilean authorities, who arrested, jailed and deported him
kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.pop: Mapuche people of the region, with several leaders supporting him
kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.laws: A hereditary constitutional monarchy created by decree
kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.challenge: Failed, as a court in Santiago declared him insane and he was expelled
kingdom-of-araucania-patagonia.recognition: None, though some Mapuche leaders supported him

kingdom-of-elleore.story: Elleore is a small island of about 15,000 square metres in Roskilde Fjord in Denmark, run as a mock kingdom by the people who own it. In 1944, during the German occupation of Denmark, a group of Copenhagen schoolteachers bought it for a summer camp. They declared it a kingdom as a gentle parody of Denmark's government and royal traditions, and gave it an invented history going back to Irish monks in the 10th century. Its place names, government bodies and noble titles imitate the Danish ones. It bans the novel Robinson Crusoe and keeps Elleore Standard Time, 12 minutes behind Danish time. The island is empty except for a week-long gathering each year called the Elleuge, attended by dozens of citizens, when the monarch is enthroned. The capital, Maglelille, is a town of tents that exists only during that week. Because the founders own the island, the project has had no conflict with the Danish state, and it continues today.
kingdom-of-elleore.mechanism: Owning land gives a group private control over how it is used, so it can run a mock kingdom there. Sovereignty, the supreme power to govern, stays with Denmark.
kingdom-of-elleore.pop: Dozens for one week each year, otherwise empty
kingdom-of-elleore.laws: Mock monarchy with nobility and a yearly enthronement
kingdom-of-elleore.challenge: Never challenged, as it is privately owned land and a parody

kingdom-of-lovely.story: The Kingdom of Lovely was a joke country created for How to Start Your Own Country, a six-part British comedy documentary shown in August and September 2005. The presenter, the comedian Danny Wallace, claimed his flat in Bow, east London, as territory, proclaimed himself king and sent a declaration of independence to the Prime Minister. The project ran partly on the internet, and at its peak 58,165 people registered as citizens on its website, citizensrequired.com, which is no longer active. A final gathering of citizens took place in Leicester Square, where Wallace revealed the country's name. Its claimed dates run from 1 January 2005 to 19 May 2013, and no state recognised it.
kingdom-of-lovely.mechanism: Declaring a flat independent has no legal effect, because the building stays under British law and the country's government.

kingdom-of-redonda.story: Redonda is an uninhabited rock just over a mile long between Nevis and Montserrat in the Caribbean, part of Antigua and Barbuda, and the subject of a literary joke about a kingdom. It has no fresh water apart from rain, and boats can land only in calm seas. From 1865 to 1912 it was mined for guano, with many thousands of tons of phosphate shipped to Britain. The writer M.P. Shiel claimed that his father, a trader from Montserrat, founded a Kingdom of Redonda in 1865, and that he himself was crowned there in 1880, though no independent evidence supports this. In 1936 Shiel passed the title and the rights to his work to the London poet John Gawsworth, who held court as King Juan in a Bayswater pub and is said to have given the title away several times when short of money. It later went to the publisher Jon Wynne-Tyson, who gave it up in 1997 in favour of the Spanish novelist Javier Marías. Marías died in 2022, and the writer Juan Gabriel Vásquez, reported as his successor, has said no official naming took place. Rival claimants still dispute the title half-seriously. In September 2023 Antigua and Barbuda created the Redonda Ecosystem Reserve across nearly 30,000 hectares, after removing goats and rats from 2016, and the island's vegetation has returned.
kingdom-of-redonda.mechanism: Passing a literary title between writers has no legal effect. Antigua and Barbuda, the country that governs the island, was able to turn it and the surrounding sea into a nature reserve without reference to any of the claimants.
kingdom-of-redonda.stopped_by: Nobody, and the titles continue among writers
kingdom-of-redonda.pop: None, as the island is nearly uninhabitable
kingdom-of-redonda.challenge: Never contested by Antigua and Barbuda, which governs the island
kingdom-of-redonda.why: Added Marías's death in 2022 and the unsettled succession; Shiel's coronation marked as unsupported.

kingdom-of-romkerhall.story: Romkerhall is a hotel and restaurant on the River Oker in the Harz Mountains of Germany, opposite an artificial waterfall about 64 metres high, and it advertises itself as a kingdom. An innkeeper named Lüer opened the first house here on 1 May 1863 on land leased from the Brunswick forestry office, and he created the waterfall that same year to draw visitors. Since 1988 the restaurant's managers have promoted the place as the "Kingdom of Romkerhall, the smallest kingdom in the world". They base this on a real feature of German local government, because the property belongs to no municipality and sits in an unincorporated area of Goslar county in Lower Saxony. An unincorporated area has no town council of its own, but it remains part of its county, its state and Germany. The title is still used to market the hotel and waterfall.
kingdom-of-romkerhall.mechanism: Land outside any town council is still inside a county and a country. Having no municipality does not remove a place from the state's authority.
kingdom-of-romkerhall.recognition: None, as this is a marketing title in Lower Saxony, Germany

kingdom-of-sedang.story: The Kingdom of Sedang was a state declared in 1888 by a French adventurer among the hill peoples of what is now central Vietnam. Charles-Marie David de Mayrena was a former French official, allegedly involved in embezzlement, who owned a plantation in French Indochina. When Siam, now Thailand, began claiming land near French holdings, he convinced a worried colonial official to send him inland to negotiate with local peoples. On arrival he persuaded the chiefs to form a kingdom under him instead. He argued that the tribes were not subjects of the emperor of Annam, the French-protected ruler of the region, and so were entitled to independence. The chiefs of the Bahnar, Rengao and Sedang elected him, and on 3 June 1888 he took the title Marie the First, with his capital at the village of Kon Gung. He offered to hand his kingdom to France in return for a trade monopoly and hinted that Prussia was interested. France did not respond positively, and Britain turned him away in Hong Kong. In Belgium in 1889 a financier offered weapons and money in exchange for mineral rights. The French Navy then blockaded Vietnamese ports and seized the arms in Singapore, so he could not return. He died on 11 November 1890 on the island of Tioman in Malaya, with reports blaming poison, a snakebite or a duel, and the kingdom ended with him.
kingdom-of-sedang.mechanism: Saying a people is independent of the nearest empire does not produce a state when a colonial power controls the sea routes and refuses recognition, meaning formal acceptance as a country.
kingdom-of-sedang.stopped_by: The French Navy, which blocked his return and seized his arms
kingdom-of-sedang.laws: Noble titles and orders handed out, and postage stamps created
kingdom-of-sedang.challenge: Failed, as France blocked him at sea
kingdom-of-sedang.recognition: None, as France did not respond positively and Britain turned him away
kingdom-of-sedang.why: Added the missing ending: Mayrena's death on Tioman in November 1890.

kingdom-of-tavolara.story: Tavolara is an island off northeast Sardinia, in Italy, whose Bertoleoni family claims it as one of the world's smallest kingdoms. The family says King Charles Albert of Sardinia approved the title, and the claim is dated to 1836, when Giuseppe Bertoleoni was head of the family. Giuseppe's son became King Paolo I in the 1840s and reigned until 1886. Italy treated the island as its own, paying 12,000 lire in 1861 for land for a lighthouse, which began operating in 1868. After 1886 newspapers reported that the island had become a republic with a president and council, but this has not been confirmed. Carlo I died in 1928, and Mariangela, aunt of the absent Paolo II, ruled as regent, or stand-in, until her death in 1934, which is said to have left the kingdom to Italy. A NATO military station was installed in 1962, the year Paolo II died. Tonino Bertoleoni, the head of the family, runs a restaurant on the island, and the family keeps up the claim.
kingdom-of-tavolara.mechanism: A family's claim that rests on an alleged royal approval has little weight when the state acts as owner. Italy bought land for a lighthouse on the island and later put a NATO base there.

kingdom-of-wallachia.story: The Kingdom of Wallachia is a joke kingdom and tourism venture in Moravian Wallachia, a region in the southeast of the Czech Republic. The photographer Tomáš Harabiš founded it in 1997 as an elaborate practical joke, and the actor Bolek Polívka was appointed King Boleslav I, with a lavish coronation in 2000. A reported 80,000 Czech citizens have acquired its passports. In 2001 Harabiš removed Polívka, accusing him of demanding one million Czech koruna for his services. Polívka said he had been king since a television show in 1993 and that most local municipalities still recognised him. Because the two could not settle it, the case went to court in Ostrava in 2007. The court ruled for Harabiš, rejecting Polívka's claim to own the "Kingdom of Wallachia" trademark and barring him from profiting from it, and a court ruled the same way in 2008. A tournament then chose a new king, Vladimír Zháněl. The kingdom has no diplomatic recognition and continues as a tourist attraction.
kingdom-of-wallachia.mechanism: When a joke kingdom's rulers fell out, the dispute was settled under ordinary Czech trademark law, which shows the kingdom was a business operating inside the state.
kingdom-of-wallachia.challenge: A leadership dispute settled in a Czech court in 2007 and 2008 as a trademark case
kingdom-of-wallachia.why: Founder identified as Tomáš Harabiš (founder field says Not stated); court dispute was a trademark case.

kiribati-natoavatu-fiji.story: This was a purchase of farmland in Fiji by the government of Kiribati, a Pacific nation of low coral islands called atolls, made with climate change in mind. In May 2014 President Anote Tong said the government had made the final payment of 8.6 million American dollars for the Natoavatu Estate on Vanua Levu, one of Fiji's islands. The 2,210-hectare property, about 22 square kilometres, had belonged to the Anglican church. Tong described it as helping Kiribati's economic and food security as the climate changed. His environment minister said at the time that they were looking for a place that could hold 60,000 or 70,000 people. Scientists disputed the reasoning, saying sand atolls can rise with the sea. Tong's successor, Taneti Maamau, later announced it would return to being a commercial farm with technical help from China, which set off rumours that it would pass to China. His office called those rumours a fabrication, and he ruled out any military use. The land remains in Fiji under Fijian law, and Kiribati holds it as an ordinary owner.
kiribati-natoavatu-fiji.mechanism: A state that buys land in another state gets ownership and no sovereignty, meaning no power to govern it. A nation losing its land would still need the host country's agreement to move its people there.
kiribati-natoavatu-fiji.recognition: Private title in Fiji, which remains the governing state
kiribati-natoavatu-fiji.cost: Final payment of 8.6 million American dollars

laas-en-bearn.story: Laàs is a village of 135 people in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques area of southwest France, between Bayonne and Pau, which declared itself a principality on 1 January 2015. The mayor, Jacques Pédéhonta, and the village were opposing the NOTRe law, a national reform of local government meant to cut administrative costs. A list of micronations describes the move as a secession over neglect by the national government, while the mayor described it as a shared dream to support the local economy. The village set up an association to give the project a legal basis, adopted a constitution, a coat of arms and a motto, and placed a customs booth at its entrance. It sells visitors a day trip that includes crossing customs, a visit to the château and lunch, and it received 28 buses in 2018. Laàs is still a French commune.
laas-en-bearn.mechanism: A village council can call itself a principality as protest and publicity. Its legal basis is an ordinary association under French law, and French sovereignty is unaffected.

add_sources.t: À Laàs, une commune de 135 habitants se rêve en principauté (Sud Radio)

ladonia.story: Ladonia is a declared country covering the area around two large sculptures in the Kullaberg nature reserve in northwest Skåne, Sweden. In 1980 the Swedish artist Lars Vilks began building them there: Nimis, made of 75 tonnes of driftwood, and Arx, made of stone. They were so hard to reach that nobody found them for two years. The local council then ruled that they were buildings, which were forbidden on the reserve, and ordered them removed. Vilks appealed repeatedly and lost. In the meantime the artist Joseph Beuys bought Nimis in 1984, and after his death the artists Christo and Jeanne-Claude bought it. On 2 June 1996, in protest against the council, Vilks declared the area an independent country called Ladonia. In 1999 he built a third sculpture, Omphalos. A foundation complained to the police, and in August 1999 a district court ordered Omphalos removed but refused to order the removal of Nimis and Arx. The foundation appealed to the Supreme Court and lost. Ladonia has a language of two words and takes citizenship applications online. It counted 22,858 citizens in 2020, none of whom live there.
ladonia.mechanism: Declaring a country can bring publicity to a planning dispute. What stayed and what went was decided under ordinary Swedish property law and by Swedish appeal courts.
ladonia.pop: No residents, with 22,858 online citizens from over 50 countries in 2020
ladonia.laws: A queen for life, an elected president and a two-word language
ladonia.challenge: Two sculptures survived court challenges, and a third was ordered removed in 1999

lanse-saint-jean.story: L'Anse-Saint-Jean is a municipality in the Saguenay region of Quebec, Canada, that made itself a joke monarchy from 1997 to 2000. On 21 January 1997 about 74 percent of residents voted in a referendum to create what was called the first municipal monarchy in America. Denys Tremblay, a professor of environmental art at the Université du Québec à Chicoutimi, was crowned King Denys I at the local church on 24 June 1997. The aim was to bring in tourists and support the local economy, with a giant artwork in plants on Mont-Édouard, depicting Saint John the Baptist and estimated to cost about a million dollars. The monarchy also proposed a municipal currency that was really a lottery ticket, and the winner could give a place in Quebec a name of their choice. Because the money for the artwork did not come, the project was dropped, and Tremblay abdicated on 14 January 2000 in a ceremony at the presbytery. The town remained a Quebec municipality throughout.
lanse-saint-jean.mechanism: A town can vote itself a title for tourism, and the vote has no effect on Canadian law or on who governs the town.
lanse-saint-jean.why: King named as Denys Tremblay; end date confirmed as 14 January 2000.

liberstad.story: Liberstad is a planned private city on three parcels of land totalling about 150 hectares in rural southern Norway, near the village of Bjelland and a few hours from Kristiansand. Its backers wanted to provide public services without a government, with minimal rules and no taxes, following the ideas of the free-market writers Mises, Hayek and Rothbard. They sold land from 2015, in bitcoin or Norwegian krone, at between about $9,400 for 1,000 square metres and $47,100 for 5,000 square metres. A company called Liberstad Drift AS was to keep the land records and act as custodian. A 2017 Cointelegraph report said development would begin on 1 June if enough plots sold. The Startup Societies Foundation, a group that promotes such projects, reported that 120 people had bought land. It said the project does not demand sovereignty of any type and described it as an experiment in how society could work. No report shows a finished settlement or a permanent population.
liberstad.mechanism: Selling plots can create a voluntary community, but buying land in Norway does not remove it from Norwegian law or tax.
liberstad.pop: 120 land buyers reported, with no residents confirmed
liberstad.currency: Cryptocurrency, with bitcoin or Norwegian krone accepted for land
liberstad.laws: Private contract rules based on a principle of non-aggression
liberstad.challenge: Not challenged, as Norwegian law still applies
liberstad.recognition: None sought, by its own account
liberstad.cost: Plots priced from $9,400 to $47,100 for 1,000 to 5,000 square metres

llanrwst-free-borough.story: Llanrwst is a town in Wales whose claim to separate status dates from the Middle Ages. In 1276 Llywelyn ap Gruffudd declared it a free borough, a town with special privileges, placing it outside the Diocese of Llanelwy, the local church district. The town defended this privilege against the Church for decades. A list of micronations gives a second date of 1947, without further explanation. Llanrwst is part of Wales and the United Kingdom.
llanrwst-free-borough.mechanism: A medieval privilege gave a town special rights against a local authority. That is a different thing from a claim to be a separate state.

malu-entu.story: The Republic of Malu Entu was a state declared on Mal di Ventre, an 81-hectare island off the west coast of Sardinia in Italy. Its leader was Salvatore "Doddore" Meloni, a former truck driver and Sardinian independence campaigner who had earlier served nine years in prison over an alleged 1980s plot to win independence with help from Libya. In September 2008 Meloni and his followers took over the island, which belonged to a British businessman, John Miller, as part of their effort to make Sardinia independent. Citing Kosovo, Abkhazia and South Ossetia as examples, he declared himself president, set up a residence in a blue plastic tent and declared the island tax-free. He sent drafts of the plan to the United Nations and to Italy's Prime Minister, Silvio Berlusconi. The occupation ended in 2009. In 2012 Meloni and five others were convicted of illegally seizing land and causing environmental damage, and he was sentenced to 20 months. He was arrested again on tax charges in April 2017, began a hunger strike and died on 5 July 2017.
malu-entu.mechanism: Occupying someone else's land and declaring a state brings ordinary criminal charges. Italian courts treated Malu Entu as an illegal seizure of private property.

add_sources.t: Sardinian independence campaigner dies after hunger strike (The Local)

malu-entu.why: Founder named as Salvatore Meloni; 2012 conviction and his 2017 death added.

maritime-republic-of-eastport.story: The Maritime Republic of Eastport is a joke country in Eastport, a waterfront neighbourhood of Annapolis, Maryland, in the United States. In January 1998 the Maryland State Highway Administration temporarily closed the drawbridge linking Eastport to the rest of the city for repairs, which threatened local shops and restaurants with losing customers. Residents came up with the idea in a pub and declared a mock secession on 25 January 1998, to encourage people to keep using Eastport's businesses. The group has kept going ever since, with an annual tug of war against Annapolis, a short run across the bridge, a yearly "Burning of the Socks" and fundraisers. Annapolis plays along with the joke, no government recognises it, and it is popular with tourists.
maritime-republic-of-eastport.mechanism: A neighbourhood can use the form of a secession to promote its businesses. No one treats it as a legal claim, and Eastport has been part of Annapolis since 1951.

murrawarri-republic.story: The Murrawarri Republic is a state declared by the Murrawarri, an Aboriginal people whose land crosses the border between Queensland and New South Wales in Australia. They released a declaration of independence on 30 March 2013 and sent it to Queen Elizabeth II, Prime Minister Julia Gillard and the two state premiers. It asked the Crown to produce one of three things: treaty documents, a deed of cession (a legal paper showing the Murrawarri gave up their sovereignty), or documents declaring war on them. Their argument was that without any of these, the Murrawarri had never lost the right to govern themselves. The Crown did not reply by the deadline of 8 May 2013, and the council took that silence to confirm continued independence. Time magazine reported that the Attorney-General's Department did not respond because it had no legal basis to do so, a view supported by the Sydney human-rights lawyer George Newhouse. A Provisional Council of State first met on 13 July 2013 at Weilmoringle, chaired by Fred Hooper. The republic's website claims 81,796 square kilometres, while a 2018 study put the area near 22,170. It uses Australian money, and the Australian government has not acknowledged it.
murrawarri-republic.mechanism: The claim rests on the fact that Aboriginal peoples signed no treaty or cession with the Crown, and it asks the Crown to prove otherwise. A government can ignore such a demand, and silence does not create independence in Australian law.
murrawarri-republic.challenge: Took its case to the United Nations in May 2013
murrawarri-republic.recognition: None, and the Australian government has not acknowledged it

north-dumpling-island.story: The Kingdom of North Dumpling is the joke name for North Dumpling Island, a two-acre island in Fishers Island Sound, in the town of Southold, New York, about a mile off the coast of Connecticut. The inventor Dean Kamen, known for the Segway, bought it in 1986 for $2.5 million. When local officials refused his request to put up a wind turbine, he declared the island's secession from the United States, though he later got permission for the turbine. He calls it a kingdom, with a constitution, a flag, a currency named the dumpling, an anthem and a navy of one amphibious vehicle. Kamen says his friendship with President George H. W. Bush produced an unofficial non-aggression pact, but this is only his own claim. The island runs on its own wind and solar power and holds an 1859 lighthouse. The secession has no legal recognition.
north-dumpling-island.mechanism: Kamen's secession was a joke protest over a refused permit. The island remains part of the United States and of Southold, New York, so its planning rules still apply.

occupation-of-alcatraz.story: The Occupation of Alcatraz was a 19-month takeover of the former prison island in San Francisco Bay, California, by Native American activists calling themselves Indians of All Tribes. The island had held Indian prisoners in the late 1800s and early 1900s, including 19 Hopi in 1895, which led one activist to say it was already Indian land in a way. In 1964 five Sicangu Lakota led by Belva Cottier landed briefly, citing the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie and raising the idea of a cultural centre and an Indian university. Richard Oakes, an Akwesasne Mohawk, and Bay Area students and urban Indians landed on 9 November 1969, and on 20 November about 100 people, 80 of them students from UCLA, began a full occupation. They wanted the deed to the island, an Indian university, a cultural centre and a museum. Oakes left after his stepdaughter died in a fall on the island in January 1970, and as students went back to school, rival groups fought for control. In mid-1970 the government offered part of Fort Miley in San Francisco, and the occupiers refused. It cut off the electricity and removed the barge that brought fresh water, and days later a fire destroyed several buildings. President Nixon approved a removal plan, and on 10 June 1971 federal marshals, FBI agents and police removed the last 15 people. The National Park Service, which now runs the island, says the occupation helped end the federal policy of terminating tribes.
occupation-of-alcatraz.mechanism: The occupiers claimed surplus federal land under old treaty ideas, and no court ever accepted that claim. The government ended the occupation by cutting off utilities and sending federal police, but the protest helped change national policy toward tribes.
occupation-of-alcatraz.stopped_by: Armed federal marshals, FBI agents and police, on 10 June 1971
occupation-of-alcatraz.pop: About 100 at the start, 15 at the end
occupation-of-alcatraz.laws: Community governance by people from many tribes
occupation-of-alcatraz.challenge: Failed, as they were removed after 19 months
occupation-of-alcatraz.why: Corrected the sequence and added demands, Fort Miley offer, reasons for decline and policy results from the National Park Service page.

orania.story: Orania is a town on the Orange River in the Northern Cape of South Africa, set up for Afrikaners, the Afrikaans-speaking white South Africans. In 1990, in the last years of apartheid, the system of legal racial separation, Carel Boshoff III and a number of families bought an abandoned workers' village. Boshoff, a son-in-law of Hendrik Verwoerd, the prime minister known as the architect of apartheid, hoped that hundreds of thousands of Afrikaners would one day live there in a state of their own, called a Volkstaat. In 2016 CNN reported about 1,300 residents, and a local census in December 2025 counted 2,903. To live there, a person must apply and be accepted as an Afrikaner, speak Afrikaans, have a clean criminal record and share the group's goals. CNN and other outside observers describe the town as whites-only, a description the community disputes. It prints money-like coupons for use in its shops, and it keeps the last transitional representative council in the country, a form of local government left over from the end of apartheid. The South African government has said it opposes a whites-only community but has generally left the town alone. After Boshoff died in 2011, his son took over the Orania Movement.
orania.mechanism: Buying land privately and controlling who may live on it can create a near-separate community under national law. This conflicts with South Africa's equality principles, but the government has chosen not to force the issue.
orania.pop: 2,903 in a local census of December 2025, up from about 1,300 in 2016
orania.laws: Entry by application, and the last transitional representative council in South Africa
orania.challenge: Not challenged directly, as the government opposes the idea but has generally left the town alone

other-world-kingdom.story: The Other World Kingdom was a commercial resort for BDSM, a form of sexual role-play based on dominance and submission, at a 16th-century château in the municipality of Černá in the Czech Republic. It was founded on 1 June 1996 and opened to visitors by spring 1997 after two years of building that cost £2 million. It presented itself as a state ruled by women under an absolute monarch, Queen Patricia I, and it claimed its own currency, passports, police, courts, flag and anthem. In fact it was a private business with no connection to any recognised state, and no country recognised it. The property was offered for sale in 2008 for eight million euros and was still for sale in 2016. As of 2020 the company still owned the building and held regular events there.
other-world-kingdom.mechanism: A private business can use the language of statehood as part of what it sells. The château stays under Czech law, and calling it a kingdom gives it no separate status.

outer-baldonia.story: Outer Baldonia was a joke principality on about 4 acres of Outer Bald Tusket Island, the southernmost of the Tusket Islands off Nova Scotia, Canada. The American businessman Russell Arundel founded it in 1949 as a private fishing retreat and took the title Prince of Princes. Its charter, now kept at the Yarmouth County Museum, covered 69 fishermen. When the Soviet publication Literaturnaya Gazeta criticised the charter, Outer Baldonia declared war on the Soviet Union on 9 March 1953, and press coverage later showed this to be a humorous half-truth. Arundel sold the island in 1973 for one Canadian dollar to the Nova Scotia Bird Society. In 2015 the Bald Islands were donated as conservation land.
outer-baldonia.mechanism: A fishing club used a charter and titles on land it owned under Canadian law. The claim lapsed when the land was sold, because it had rested on ownership alone.
outer-baldonia.cost: Sold for one Canadian dollar in 1973

parva-domus.story: Parva Domus Magna Quies is a private social club in the Punta Carretas neighbourhood of Montevideo, Uruguay, that calls itself a republic. Its Latin name means small house, big rest. On 25 August 1878 fishermen tired of carrying their gear to the beach bought a small shack for storage and meetings and declared it a republic as a joke. It has a president elected every two years, a cabinet of ministers, a flag and an anthem, and it marches in costume on its Independence Day each August. Its creed is pleasure and friendship. Members avoid talking about religion, politics and sport, and anyone who loses their temper can be put in a mock jail. Membership is all male, limited to 250, and drawn from wealthy professionals such as doctors, lawyers and politicians. In 2007 it hosted informal talks between Argentine and Uruguayan diplomats during a dispute over a pulp mill. It is legally registered in Uruguay as a cultural association, and it has no official recognition as a state.
parva-domus.mechanism: A club can use the forms of a republic for fun while being, in law, an ordinary cultural association registered with the state.

add_sources.t: The Uruguayan micronation where fun is the goal (Buenos Aires Times)

parva-domus.why: Founders identified as fishermen buying a shack; founder field says Not stated.

pescenica.story: The Republic of Peščenica was a satirical country set in Peščenica, a suburb of Zagreb, the capital of Croatia. Željko Malnar, a Croatian traveller, writer and television personality, proclaimed it on 3 October 1992 and named himself president. It grew out of his weekly television show Nightmare Stage, which featured colourful characters from the streets of Zagreb, and it was used to mock Croatian politics. The show ended on 26 June 2010, which is the end date a list of micronations gives for the republic. Malnar's biography has him holding the title until his death on 9 July 2013.
pescenica.mechanism: A television joke can use the form of a state to mock politics. It makes no legal claim that a government would have to answer.
pescenica.why: End date moved to 2013: the show ended in 2010, but Malnar held the title until his death in July 2013.

principality-of-filettino.story: Filettino is a village of about 554 people, some 70 kilometres east of Rome in Italy, that announced in 2011 it would become an independent principality. The Italian government had passed an austerity package of about 50 billion euros, which required towns of fewer than 1,000 people to merge with their neighbours. The mayor, Luca Sellari, would have lost his job under the plan, and he wanted the town to keep managing its own land, forests and water. So he led a campaign to make Filettino a self-governing principality, pointing to the many small states that existed before Italy was unified. The town printed a currency called the fiorito with his picture on it and sold T-shirts with a new coat of arms. Not everyone agreed, and a local restaurant owner said residents wanted to run their own resources but not to leave Italy. By November 2011 the merger had still not gone ahead, although the government was pressing the town to share services. No report says what became of the principality after that.
principality-of-filettino.mechanism: A mayor's declaration can draw attention to a national law, but it does not stop that law from applying. Only the Italian parliament and government can decide how towns are organised.

add_sources.t: Euro Crisis Prompts Italian Village to Declare Independence (VOA)

principality-of-freedonia.story: The Principality of Freedonia was a plan to found a libertarian country, one with minimal government, based in Boston, Massachusetts, in the United States. A group of American teenagers began it in 1992 as a hypothetical project and made it a formal plan for a new country in 1997, headed by a Texas university student named John Kyle, who used the title Prince John. It minted its own silver coins and sold them online. In 2001 it tried to lease land in Somaliland, a self-governing region of Somalia, but the attempt was rejected. It never gained territory beyond one leader's home. The founder said in 2004 that the project was no longer being pursued, and its website had gone by 2013.
principality-of-freedonia.mechanism: A new country needs land before anything else. Freedonia's only reported attempt to lease some was refused, and owning a house in Boston gave it no separate status.

principality-of-marlborough.story: The Principality of Marlborough was a short-lived state declared in 1993 near Marlborough, Queensland, Australia, about 106 kilometres north of Rockhampton. George Muirhead, a grazier, or livestock farmer, was facing the repossession of two rural properties. He declared them independent, named himself Duke of Marlborough and held a ceremony under four flags, those of Australia, the Aboriginal people, Scotland and the United Nations. Police evicted him and his family eleven days later, and Sydney newspapers reported in June 1993 that he and others had been jailed for contempt of court over the land.
principality-of-marlborough.mechanism: A declaration of independence does not stop a lender repossessing land. Australian police and courts enforced the repossession within days.
principality-of-marlborough.why: Position replaced with published coordinates (22°30'18"S 149°9'6"E). Founder is George Muirhead (founder field says Not stated).

principality-of-seborga.story: Seborga is a village in Liguria, northwest Italy, near the French border and about 35 kilometres from Monaco, that calls itself a principality. In 1963 Giorgio Carbone, a former flower grower who headed the local growers' cooperative, said documents in the Vatican archives showed Seborga had never belonged to the House of Savoy, the royal family that united Italy. So, he argued, it was wrongly included in the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. Supporters add that the Congress of Vienna, the 1815 meeting that redrew Europe's borders, overlooked it. None of these claims has been proved. Villagers elected Carbone head of state that year, and he took the title His Tremendousness, Giorgio I. He formed a cabinet, minted a currency called the luigino, and adopted a blue and white flag and the Latin motto Sub Umbra Sede, meaning sit in the shade. Sentry boxes stand on the road into the village. He held the role until he died in 2009. Marcello Menegatto was elected in 2010 and Nina Menegatto in 2019, with a further seven-year term confirmed on 23 October 2026. Italy continues to run the village as an ordinary comune, or municipality, in Imperia province, and tourism has grown.
principality-of-seborga.mechanism: A historical argument about a lost state, even with strong local support, changes nothing in law while the national government goes on running the place as an ordinary municipality.
principality-of-seborga.pop: 283 in 2025, in an ordinary Italian town
principality-of-seborga.laws: A prince elected by the town, with ministers and a motto
principality-of-seborga.challenge: No court test is reported, and the town remains an Italian municipality
principality-of-seborga.recognition: None confirmed, though supporters claim recognition by Burkina Faso

principality-of-wy.story: The Principality of Wy is a family house in the Sydney suburb of Mosman, Australia, whose owner declared it independent of the local council. In 1993 the Delprat family applied to build a driveway across an unbuilt road to reach their home, which began a long dispute with Mosman Council. On 15 November 2004 the artist Paul Delprat declared that he had seceded from Mosman, though not from Australia, and named himself Prince. The fight over the driveway carried on under ordinary planning law, and after 20 years of seeking permission he lost his court appeal in 2013. In the meantime the principality drew coverage from newspapers and broadcasters in several countries, and Delprat attended the first Australian conference of micronation leaders in 2010. It supports the arts and sponsors an art prize. It has no local, national or international recognition, and the family never got its driveway.
principality-of-wy.mechanism: Declaring secession from a council has no effect on planning law. The council's decision was tested and upheld through an ordinary appeal.
principality-of-wy.laws: Royal titles and support for the arts

province-of-bumbunga.story: The Province of Bumbunga was a farm near Snowtown and Lochiel in South Australia that its owner declared independent so that it could stay loyal to the British Crown. Alec Brackstone, a British monarchist and former postmaster and prospector, feared that Australia was moving toward becoming a republic after the Governor-General, the Queen's representative, dismissed Prime Minister Gough Whitlam's government in November 1975. On 29 March 1976 he declared the property independent and appointed himself governor-general. To draw tourists he planted thousands of strawberry plants in the shape of Great Britain and planned weddings on soil from British counties, but Australian customs seized the soil and the plants later died in a drought. From 1980 he issued collectors' stamps with no postal value, mostly showing the royal family. Changes to investment law in 1987 made these less attractive, and he gave up the business. In 1999 he was charged with illegally possessing firearms, and his claim to diplomatic immunity failed, though he says the charges were later dropped. The claim is usually dated as ending about 2000, but Brackstone was still calling himself its governor in 2018.
province-of-bumbunga.mechanism: Brackstone seceded in order to stay under the Crown, the reverse of the usual claim. Australian customs and courts went on treating him as any other Australian resident.

set.anchor: Bumbunga, near Snowtown and Lochiel, South Australia

province-of-bumbunga.why: Founder named as Alec Brackstone (founder field says Not stated); reason and events added.

rainbow-creek.story: The Independent State of Rainbow Creek was a farm at Cowwarr, on the Thomson River in Victoria, Australia, that seceded from the state of Victoria over flooding. In 1952 the river cut a new course around a badly placed bridge, forming Rainbow Creek. Later floods widened it, and a weir built upstream in 1954 sent more water into it, so farmers lost land and infrastructure while still paying levies to the council and water authorities. Thomas Barnes, a retired British and Victorian police officer who owned the Yammacoona property, led the farmers. When they were refused compensation in 1978, Barnes and about thirty others signed a declaration of war on Victoria and served it on the state governor before television cameras in January 1979. They rejected a government offer of loans. On 23 July 1979 Barnes declared Yammacoona seceded from Victoria, named himself Governor and swore allegiance to Queen Elizabeth II, in imitation of Hutt River. The state issued passports, stamps and banknotes to publicise the farmers' cause. Barnes retired to Queensland in the mid-1980s because of ill health, and the flooding dispute was never resolved.
rainbow-creek.mechanism: This was a secession from one Australian state, made to win compensation, and it kept loyalty to the Crown. It gained publicity but no change in the law that governed the farm.
rainbow-creek.why: Founder named as Thomas Barnes; the dispute was over flood damage and levies; site confirmed as Cowwarr, so the point was moved (coordinates are approximate for the town, not from a retrieved page).

republic-of-kugelmugel.story: The Republic of Kugelmugel is a spherical house eight metres across that its builder declared an independent country, now standing in the Prater park in Vienna, Austria. In 1971 the artist Edwin Lipburger and his son built it near Wiener Neustadt in Lower Austria without a building permit, which started a long dispute with the authorities. In August 1975 the township of Neudorfl offered it a home, and moving it by helicopter was discussed, but that did not happen. Lipburger then declared the sphere an independent republic, with the date given as 19 December 1976, and issued passports. In 1979 he was sentenced to 10 weeks in prison for unlawful assumption of a public authority, the Austrian offence of acting as an official without the right to. In 1982 the building was dismantled and moved to the Prater, where it sits behind tall barbed-wire fences. Helmut Zilk, who became mayor of Vienna in 1984, gave it what was called asylum. The city assumed the arrangement would be temporary, and the legal dispute continued. The republic claims 94 square metres and has a single address, 2 Antifaschismusplatz. Nikolaus Lipburger took over in 2015, and Linda Treiber became president in 2022.
republic-of-kugelmugel.mechanism: Declaring a building a state does not cure a planning violation. When the founder acted as if he held public office, Austria used a criminal offence against false official acts.
republic-of-kugelmugel.pop: Nobody is confirmed as living there
republic-of-kugelmugel.challenge: The founder was jailed for 10 weeks in 1979, and the city later gave the building "asylum"

republic-of-lakotah.story: The Republic of Lakotah was a proposed country for the Lakota, a Native American people, covering thousands of square miles in North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Wyoming and Montana. On 17 December 2007 four activists calling themselves the Lakota Freedom Delegation went to Washington, D.C., and contacted the State Department. Their leader was Russell Means, a long-time member of the American Indian Movement, who called himself chief facilitator of a provisional government. They said the Lakota were withdrawing from the treaties their ancestors had signed with the United States, citing what they called the colonial apartheid of the reservation system, along with unemployment, poverty, disease and repeated treaty violations. Their borders followed the 1851 Treaty of Fort Laramie, on land that now holds reservations and non-Native towns. The State Department referred questions elsewhere, and a Bureau of Indian Affairs official said the withdrawal did not mean anything. No recognised Lakota tribal government had been consulted or backed the plan, and the Rosebud Sioux and Cheyenne River chairmen said so publicly. In 2008 the group filed liens, or legal claims on property, on federal land in a South Dakota county, and these were rejected. It asked embassies for recognition without success. Means ran for president of the Pine Ridge Reservation that year, treating the vote as a test of support, and lost 2,277 to 1,918. Nothing significant is reported after that.
republic-of-lakotah.mechanism: A claim based on treaties made with a named people has a stronger history behind it than a flag on empty land. A withdrawal from those treaties still needs backing from that people's own governments and a state willing to respond.
republic-of-lakotah.laws: A provisional government named by the delegation
republic-of-lakotah.challenge: Never tested in court, and its property claims in South Dakota were rejected
republic-of-lakotah.recognition: None, and the recognised Lakota tribal governments did not support it
republic-of-lakotah.why: Added the 2008 events and named government and tribal responses; outcome now stated.

republic-of-madawaska.story: The Republic of Madawaska was a self-declared state on the Saint John River, in the area where Maine in the United States meets New Brunswick and Quebec in Canada. The 1783 Treaty of Paris defined the border between the United States and British North America imprecisely, so both sides claimed this area, where a mainly French-speaking settlement had 2,487 people in 1830. John Baker, an American settler, arrived in 1817 and lived near what is now Baker Brook. In 1825 he asked Maine to take the settlement in. Convinced that the land was American, he began provoking the British, trying in 1827 to stop mail being carried by canoe to Quebec and urging French residents to reject British authority. A republic was declared on 4 July 1827, with Baker given the title General. He was arrested on 25 September and spent 13 months in jail in Fredericton, and a jury convicted him of opposing British authority and fined him £25. The border dispute went on until the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 settled it, dividing the communities between New Brunswick, Maine and Quebec. The republic was claimed without ever being shown to work as a government, though its flag still flies in Edmundston, New Brunswick.
republic-of-madawaska.mechanism: Where two states claim the same land, supporters of one side can declare a republic to put pressure on the other. Here the other state ended it with an arrest and a trial, and a treaty between the two states settled the border.
republic-of-madawaska.pop: The Madawaska settlement had 2,487 people in 1830
republic-of-madawaska.challenge: Failed, as its leader was arrested within three months
republic-of-madawaska.why: Treaty year, the 1842 treaty name, and Baker's trial and sentence added.

republic-of-molossia.story: Molossia is 11.3 acres of private land near Dayton, Nevada, in the United States, whose owner Kevin Baugh runs it as a joke country and calls himself President. He thought up the idea as a teenager in 1977 with a friend, under other names including the Grand Republic of Vuldstein, and it took its present form after he bought the land in 1998. He credits the film The Mouse That Roared and his time in the army. Visitors pay a customs fee of pocket change, have their passports stamped and receive money made of paper circles on poker chips. The currency is the Valora, set at 80 American cents. Laws ban onions, spinach and catfish, and setting off a nuclear device carries a 500 Valora fine. It says it has been in a conflict with East Germany since 1983, because of drills Baugh did in the army. The Independent reported 27 citizens. No member of the United Nations recognises it. Baugh pays property tax to Storey County and calls this foreign aid, so the county has no dispute with him.
republic-of-molossia.mechanism: Owning land and paying local tax on it, even under a joke label, avoids the conflict with the state that ended other claims. The state has no reason to act when its taxes are paid.
republic-of-molossia.laws: A president, a flag and joke laws
republic-of-molossia.challenge: None, as Baugh pays local property tax
republic-of-molossia.recognition: None by any member of the United Nations

republic-of-montmartre.story: The Republic of Montmartre is a charitable association of artists in the Montmartre district of Paris, France, run in the style of a mock republic. It was created in 1921 to protect the character of Montmartre from property developers after the First World War and to keep alive the artists' habit of helping one another. The City of Paris credits the illustrator Joe Bridge with proposing it on 7 May 1921, while a list of micronations names the cartoonist Jean Barrez. It has a president, ministers, ambassadors and more than 500 volunteer members, who wear a red scarf, black cape and black hat. Its motto means doing good with joy. It holds Christmas celebrations for local children, gives money to groups that work with disadvantaged children, and runs exhibitions, book fairs and concerts, and it remains active today.
republic-of-montmartre.mechanism: An association can take the form of a republic for fun and fundraising. It has no separate status in French law.

add_sources.t: La République de Montmartre (Ville de Paris)

republic-of-montmartre.why: Sources disagree on the proposer: the City of Paris credits Joe Bridge in May 1921; the micronation list says Jean Barrez in 1920. Founder field still says Jean Barrez.

republic-of-saugeais.story: Le Saugeais is a wooded valley in the Haut-Doubs in eastern France, along the Swiss border, that has called itself a republic since a lunchtime joke in 1947. Louis Ottaviani, the senior government official for the Doubs region, stopped to eat at a restaurant by the abbey in Montbenoit. The owner, Georges Pourchet, jokingly asked whether he had a permit to enter the territory of Le Saugeais. Ottaviani played along, saying such a place sounded like a republic, that a republic needs a president, and that Pourchet was it. In May 1972 the abbey's priest and the mayor told Gabrielle, the mother of Georgette Bertin-Pourchet, that the citizens wanted her to take over. A flag based on the old colours of Franche-Comté followed in 1981 and a postage stamp in 1987. Georgette Bertin-Pourchet later became president by unanimous vote, and on 18 March 2022, aged 88, she handed the post to her prime minister, Simon Marguet. The government also has a secretary-general, two customs officers and ambassadors. France does not recognise the republic.
republic-of-saugeais.mechanism: A joke started by a government official has no legal effect. A local identity can last more than 70 years this way without changing national law.
republic-of-saugeais.pop: Valley residents, in numbers not confirmed
republic-of-saugeais.laws: A president, a prime minister, a secretary-general, two customs officers and ambassadors

republic-of-texas-group.story: The Republic of Texas is a movement in the American state of Texas which says the state's 1845 annexation by the United States was illegal and that Texas is still an independent nation under occupation. Richard Lance McLaren started it and claimed to have restored a provisional government on 13 December 1995. He argued that Texas had been a captive nation of war since 1865, a claim scholars do not support. The movement split into three factions in 1996, and activists claim more than 40,000 supporters. In 1997 McLaren and his followers kidnapped Joe and Margaret Ann Rowe, held them at the Davis Mountain Resort and demanded the release of a movement member in exchange. A week-long standoff with police and Texas Rangers followed, until McLaren's wife Evelyn convinced him to give up. He and four others went to prison, and his projected release date is 2041. Two members slipped away, and Rangers shot Mike Matson dead two days later. Richard Keyes III surrendered that September and was sentenced in June 1998 to 90 years. That year a federal court ruled that the Republic of Texas no longer exists. Remaining groups joined under an interim government in 2003, and in 2015 federal and state officers raided a meeting of about sixty followers but made no arrests.
republic-of-texas-group.mechanism: When a legal theory of secession turns to hostage-taking, ordinary criminal law decides the outcome. A federal court separately ruled that the old republic no longer exists.
republic-of-texas-group.pop: Followers at a compound in the Davis Mountains, with claims of 40,000 supporters statewide
republic-of-texas-group.challenge: Failed, with leaders jailed after a week-long standoff and a 1998 federal ruling against the claim
republic-of-texas-group.why: Added the 1998 federal court ruling, Matson's death and activity to 2015. The end year of 1998 marks McLaren's group; other factions were still active in 2015.

republic-of-uzupis.story: Užupis is a neighbourhood of about 60 hectares in Vilnius, the capital of Lithuania, that artists declared an independent republic as a local celebration. Its name means beyond the river, because it lies on the far side of the Vilnele river. In 1995 local artists used an empty Soviet-era plinth for a statue of Frank Zappa, and on 1 April 1997 they declared the district an independent republic. It has a president, Romas Lileikis, a government, and a navy of three or four small boats used for ceremonies. An army of about 10 men has been retired. Lileikis and a colleague named Cepaitis wrote the constitution in about three hours one afternoon in 1998. It has 41 clauses, including a right to hot water because Lileikis had none that day, and it has been translated into many languages. On Užupis Day, 1 April, visitors can have their passports stamped. Foreign governments do not recognise the republic, and no dispute with the Lithuanian state is reported. It has become a source of pride in Vilnius.
republic-of-uzupis.mechanism: A state can treat a self-declared republic as local culture at no cost, because the claim expresses an identity and leaves law and taxes as they were.
republic-of-uzupis.laws: A 41-clause constitution, a president and a government
republic-of-uzupis.challenge: No challenge reported, as it is accepted as a local tradition

republic-of-vevcani.story: Vevcani is a village of about 2,400 people near Lake Ohrid in North Macedonia that has declared independence more than once. It first threatened to secede from Yugoslavia in 1987. In 1991, during the break-up of Yugoslavia, it proclaimed itself an independent republic 11 days after the Yugoslav republic of Macedonia declared its own independence. In 2002 locals revived the idea as a light-hearted way to draw tourists and poke fun at politics, by flying a national flag, issuing passports and printing money. The village's springs are at the centre of its customs and celebrations, and they are promoted to visitors. North Macedonia continues to govern the village as part of its territory.
republic-of-vevcani.mechanism: A secession bid made while a federation, a union of self-governing republics, is breaking up can turn into a tourist brand once the new national state is firmly in place.
republic-of-vevcani.challenge: No state response is reported, and it was a tourist tradition by 2002

rough-and-ready.story: Rough and Ready is a small town in California, in the United States, which declared itself a separate country for less than three months in 1850. It was settled in fall 1849 by a Wisconsin mining company led by Captain A. A. Townsend, who named it after General Zachary Taylor. On 7 April 1850 the town declared secession from the Union as the Great Republic of Rough and Ready, largely to avoid taxes on mining. Residents voted to rejoin the United States on 4 July that year. The town still celebrates the republic each year for tourism and local pride, and it had 905 people in the 2020 census.
rough-and-ready.mechanism: Secession in a remote mining camp lasted only until residents voted to rejoin. Because they gave it up themselves, no court ever had to rule on it.

ruterberg.story: Rüterberg is a village on the Elbe River in northern Germany that declared itself a republic on the eve of the fall of the Berlin Wall. It lay in East Germany, on the stretch of river that formed the border with West Germany, and by the end of the communist period a wall surrounded it and cut it off from the rest of East Germany. From 1988 local residents, led by Hans Rasenberger, discussed creating a free town with its own laws, breaking ties with East Germany. An assembly of 90 citizens proclaimed the republic on 8 November 1989. The Berlin Wall fell the next day, and the village became part of reunified Germany. On 14 July 1991 the state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern acknowledged the people's right to use the title Dorfrepublik, or Village Republic. It is now part of the town of Dömitz.
ruterberg.mechanism: This local declaration was overtaken within a day by the collapse of the state it opposed. Later the new state government allowed the title as an honour, with no change in who governs the village.

shanhaiwoo.story: ShanhaiWoo is a pop-up city, a temporary community that gathers in one place for a limited period and calls itself a city. A list of such gatherings by the newsletter Agartha places it in China and Thailand, and a report by IOSG counts it among the communities that met in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in October 2024. Neither names its founders or says how many people attended, and no report says what it has done since.
shanhaiwoo.mechanism: A temporary gathering of visitors stays under the law of the host country and makes no claim on its territory.

slowjamastan.story: Slowjamastan is a patch of private desert in Imperial County, California, in the United States, that its owner declared an independent country. The DJ Randy Williams visited the joke country of Molossia in August 2021, then bought 11.07 acres for $19,000 that October and declared independence on 1 December. He calls himself sultan and describes the government as a dictatorship with occasional democracy. A border sign and post stand beside State Route 78, with a desk serving as the sultan's office. Nobody lived there as of February 2025, while more than 25,000 citizens had applied online by March 2026. Passports carry quotations from hip hop artists, and the currency is the duble. Williams bases his claim on the Montevideo Convention, a treaty that lists the features of a state such as territory and a government. Slowjamastan has no legal recognition.
slowjamastan.mechanism: Owning land gives the right to use it, and it does not end the authority of the government over it. California and American law continue to apply.
slowjamastan.pop: Over 25,000 online citizens (March 2026), with no residents (February 2025)

snake-hill.story: The Principality of Snake Hill is a self-declared country near Mudgee in New South Wales, Australia, started by a family in debt. The Jensen family could no longer afford their taxes and had been in court over a mortgage. Inspired by the Hutt River farm in Western Australia, they declared independence on 2 September 2003, claiming land the size of Monaco. Helena Jensen took over the leadership after her husband Paul died in 2010. The money problems continued, and in 2011 the Bank of Queensland foreclosed on, or took back, their home, which they called their embassy. They tried to block the sale by arguing that the bank's action was a matter for international law and for the High Court of Australia or the International Court of Justice, but a judge of the New South Wales Supreme Court dismissed these claims in February 2011. Their daughter Paula appeared often in the state's courts until 2014. No government recognises Snake Hill.
snake-hill.mechanism: Declaring independence does not cancel a mortgage or a tax bill. A New South Wales court ruled that the bank's foreclosure was an ordinary matter for Australian courts.
snake-hill.why: Site now identified as near Mudgee, so the point was moved (coordinates are approximate for the town, not from a retrieved page). Founders are the Jensen family (founder field says Not stated). The 2011 foreclosure and court loss are added.

sovereign-yidindji-government.story: The Sovereign Yidindji Government is a government set up by members of the Yidindji, an Aboriginal people of northern Queensland in Australia, who renounced their legal ties with Australia in 2014 (a list of micronations says 2013). Gudju Gudju Gimuybara is chief minister and Murrumu Walubara Yidindji is foreign and trade minister. It claims about 2,500 square kilometres south of Port Douglas, through Cairns and inland across the Atherton Tablelands, plus 80 kilometres of sea. It issues its own driver's licences. In May 2015 Queensland police charged Murrumu after finding him with a licence and number plates from the Yidindji government, and he argued that the police had no jurisdiction, or legal authority, over him. No report says how the case ended. In 2022 the group launched a digital Sovereign Yidindji Dollar, pegged to the Australian dollar. It hopes for a formal agreement with the Australian government and has approached Russia and Venezuela.
sovereign-yidindji-government.mechanism: Issuing its own licences brought the claim into a traffic court, where Australian law meets the assertion of sovereignty. A sovereignty claim is tested when someone acts on it in daily life.
sovereign-yidindji-government.challenge: A Queensland traffic charge in May 2015, with no outcome reported

sultanate-of-msimbati.story: The Sultanate of M'Simbati was a private estate in what is now Tanzania, about 25 kilometres southeast of Mtwara, whose English owner declared it independent. Latham Leslie-Moore, a former British artillery officer, bought the property at auction in the 1940s, when the area was the British colony of Tanganyika. In 1959 he declared it separate and named himself sultan, and he wrote to the colonial governors asking for recognition, meaning acceptance as a state. After Tanganyika and Zanzibar joined to form Tanzania, he wrote to President Julius Nyerere and the United Nations as well. None of them recognised it. A list of micronations gives 1980 as its end, and ruins of its so-called palace remain.
sultanate-of-msimbati.mechanism: A landowner can ask for recognition, but no government has to give it. First the colonial rulers and then independent Tanzania treated the estate as part of their territory.

set.anchor: Msimbati, Tanzania, about 25 km southeast of Mtwara

sunda-empire.story: The Sunda Democratic Empire was an invented empire based in Bandung, Indonesia, claiming to succeed the empire of Alexander the Great and to have authority over all countries. It grew from claims made around 2003 by Nasri Banks and his wife Raden Ratna Ningrum, who gave money to a man offering a supposed bank deposit of 2 billion dollars. In 2007 their daughters were detained in Malaysia for trying to enter with Sunda Empire diplomatic passports. They refused to accept Indonesian citizenship, so Malaysia treated them as stateless and kept them in an immigration depot. In early 2020 a video spread online showing Rangga Sasana, calling himself secretary general, inviting all countries to register with the empire, which he said would settle their debts to the World Bank. Police arrested the leaders for fraud that January. At trial Nasri said the declaration was an attempt to have his daughters sent home. All three were sentenced to two years in prison for spreading false information and disturbing the peace, and they were freed in 2021 under a pandemic release policy. Rangga Sasana died in December 2022.
sunda-empire.mechanism: Indonesian authorities did not need to rule on the empire's history. They prosecuted its leaders under ordinary law for spreading false information.
sunda-empire.why: Leaders named (Nasri Banks, Raden Ratna Ningrum, Rangga Sasana). The Alexander claim came from Ratna, and the group was publicly declared in 2020.

telosa.story: Telosa is a proposed new city in the United States that has not been built. In September 2021 the billionaire Marc Lore, a former Walmart executive, announced a plan for a city on 150,000 acres of cheap land, at a stated cost of $400 billion. It would hold 5 million people, by 2050 in some reports and over 40 years in others. A first phase would house 50,000 people on 1,500 acres at over $25 billion. Lore's idea of how to pay for it comes from the economist Henry George, who argued that land value should benefit the community. People could be licensed to build on and sell structures while residents shared ownership of the land through a community endowment, a fund held for all of them. Fossil-fuel vehicles would be banned, and the architects Bjarke Ingels Group drew the plan. No site had been chosen, with Nevada, Utah, Arizona, Idaho, Texas and the Appalachian region named as options, and no construction is reported.
telosa.mechanism: A private buyer can plan a city on land it buys, but the land stays under state and national law. Telosa does not ask to be anything other than an American city.
telosa.recognition: None sought, as it is a planned American city
telosa.cost: $400 billion proposed, with over $25 billion for the first phase

set.anchor: Nevada, one of several states named as options; no site chosen

vemerana.story: Vemerana was a breakaway state declared in 1980 on Espiritu Santo, an island in the Pacific country of Vanuatu, which until that year was the New Hebrides, ruled jointly by Britain and France. Jimmy Stevens led Nagriamel, a conservative movement on the island, and he and his allies opposed the plans for independence after losing recent elections. Michael Oliver's Phoenix Foundation, an American libertarian group already behind attempts to create new states at Minerva and Abaco, wanted a tax haven in the islands and supported him. In 1980 his followers blockaded the airport, destroyed two bridges and declared the State of Vemerana. The government asked Britain and France for troops. France refused to let its soldiers act against the rebels and was later found to have secretly supported Stevens. Vanuatu became independent on 30 July 1980. Walter Lini, its incoming prime minister, asked Papua New Guinea for help, and that country sent troops in its first overseas deployment. The rebels had mainly bows, rocks and slings, and there were few casualties. In late August soldiers killed Stevens's son at a roadblock, and on 28 August Stevens surrendered. His trial revealed that he and Nagriamel had received 250,000 American dollars from the Phoenix Foundation. He was sentenced to 14 years, was freed in 1991 and died in 1994.
vemerana.mechanism: A newly independent government used soldiers from a neighbouring state to end a privately funded secession. Recognised governments can call on one another against such claims.
vemerana.stopped_by: The government of Vanuatu, with troops from Papua New Guinea
vemerana.challenge: None in court, as the revolt ended in August 1980 and Stevens was jailed
vemerana.cost: 250,000 American dollars from the Phoenix Foundation to Stevens and Nagriamel, revealed at his trial
vemerana.why: Added French support, the end of the revolt and independence date. Dropped an uncited allegation about arms and casino concessions.

vikesland.story: The Kingdom of Vikesland was a micronation, a self-declared country that no government recognises, in Brandon, Manitoba, Canada. A television news cameraman founded it in 2005 for a documentary about micronations, and it claimed his home and a property he owned jointly with someone else. It lasted until 2018. No report gives any response from the Canadian government.
vikesland.mechanism: Calling a home and a jointly owned plot a kingdom has no legal effect in Canada, where ordinary property law continues to apply.

vitalia.story: Vitalia was a temporary village focused on longevity, the science of living longer, held in February 2024 in Próspera, a zone in Honduras with its own legal rules. It had a laboratory for biohacking, meaning self-experiment to improve the body, along with workout groups and a biomedical hackathon, a contest to build projects quickly. Its organisers hoped it would lead to a permanent home base, and it is listed as a spin-off of Zuzalu, an earlier pop-up village. It ended after its 2024 session, and no report shows a permanent base.
