vitalia.mechanism: Vitalia used a zone with its own legal rules to host experiments, so its standing depends on how Honduras treats Próspera. The village made no claim of its own to govern land.

whangamomona.story: Whangamomona is a small settlement in the interior of New Zealand's North Island that declared itself a republic in protest at a change of local boundaries. Its statistical area covers about 690 square kilometres and had 159 people in the 2023 census. In local government reforms in 1989 it was placed in the Manawatu-Wanganui Region, on the grounds that the Whangamomona River flows into the Whanganui River. Residents wanted to be in the Taranaki Region. On 1 November 1989, at what they called the first Republic Day, they responded by declaring the Republic of Whangamomona. The declaration began as a pointed protest, and the town kept up the event as a yearly celebration with a vote for president. It became a festival that draws visitors from across the North Island, and in 2001 it moved to every two years, held in January for better weather. No formal response from the New Zealand government is reported. The republic continues as a local festival.
whangamomona.mechanism: An argument over which regional council governs a town can become a lasting local identity. The town stays fully under New Zealand law.
whangamomona.laws: A president chosen by vote on Republic Day
whangamomona.challenge: No challenge reported, as it is a festival

winneconne-sovereign-state.story: Winneconne is a village in Wisconsin, in the United States, that declared itself a separate state for a day in 1967 after being left off the official map. Wisconsin's 1967 highway map showed no name for the village, and residents feared losing tourist money. Governor Warren Knowles said the map could not be redrawn and promised a fix in 1968. Vera Kitchen, president of the Chamber of Commerce, a local business group, ran a contest called Here's How to Put Winneconne Back on the Map, which drew over 1,000 entries. Two congressional aides in Washington won with a plan for secession and war. The village took up the secession, delivered a declaration to the governor on 22 July 1967, lowered the state flag and raised a banner showing a skunk, a sheepshead fish, poison ivy and a dodo. Parades, boat races and a one-day toll bridge followed. Knowles phoned that day with the state's regrets, and the secession ended within 24 hours. The village has celebrated Sovereign State Days nearly every year since.
winneconne-sovereign-state.mechanism: This was a publicity stunt to get attention from the state. It ended with a phone call, and nobody pressed any legal claim.

zad-notre-dame-des-landes.story: The ZAD of Notre-Dame-des-Landes was a long occupation of a farming area of 1,650 hectares near Nantes in France, set up to stop a planned airport. The French state had planned the airport there since the 1960s, and local farmers and environmental groups fought it for decades. In the 2000s squatters occupied much of the land, while farmers refused to leave. The occupiers named it a Zone to Defend, or ZAD in French, and set up their own communal bakery, livestock farming and other shared structures. Attempts to clear the area drew large public protests in 2012 and 2018. On 17 January 2018 Prime Minister Edouard Philippe announced that the airport would be dropped and the existing Nantes airport redeveloped. The state then evicted part of the occupation in 2018, and many of the remaining projects went through a process of legalisation, moving from occupation to ordinary French land and farm law. The occupiers stopped the airport, and those who stayed did so under permissions from the state.
zad-notre-dame-des-landes.mechanism: A long occupation can stop a state project and win a negotiated right to stay. The price is accepting legal status under that same state.
zad-notre-dame-des-landes.stopped_by: French state evictions in 2018, after which the remaining projects took legal status
zad-notre-dame-des-landes.challenge: Blocked an airport, then was partly evicted and partly legalised
zad-notre-dame-des-landes.recognition: The French government accepted some projects after 2018

zapatista-territories.story: The Zapatista autonomous territories are communities in Chiapas, one of Mexico's poorest states, that have governed themselves outside the Mexican state since 1994. On 1 January 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement took effect, masked Mayan farmers of the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) briefly seized several cities in Chiapas. Their name honours Emiliano Zapata, a hero of the 1910 revolution. The fighting stopped, and they kept control of their own communities. Until 2003 these were organised around community centres called Aguascalientes. These were then replaced by regional centres called Caracoles, with autonomous municipalities run by Councils of Good Government. Al Jazeera reported from the village of Oventic in 2014 that the Zapatistas governed and policed their own communities across five regions and that relations with the state stayed strained. In 2023, after a rise in cartel violence, the EZLN announced that the autonomous municipalities would dissolve and be replaced by Local Autonomous Governments, grouped in collectives and regional assemblies. No state recognises the territories as a separate country, and the Zapatistas operate inside Mexico.
zapatista-territories.mechanism: A rural movement backed by armed force can hold real self-government for decades without any legal status, by running its own communities without formally seceding.
zapatista-territories.laws: Councils of Good Government until 2023, and Local Autonomous Governments since
zapatista-territories.challenge: Has survived since the 1994 uprising, with relations with the state still strained

zaqistan.story: Zaqistan is a four-acre patch of desert in northwestern Box Elder County, Utah, in the United States, which its owner calls a country. Zaq Landsberg, a New York resident, bought the land online in about 2005, having seen it only as coordinates on a GPS, and he calls himself its president. He has set up a flag, a border gate, a supply bunker, a robot sentry and official-looking passports, which visitors can have stamped. The site is about 60 miles from the nearest town, and its exact location is kept private. Landsberg describes it as an art project that tests the limits of land ownership and sovereignty, and he admits it is unlikely to become a real country. No other country recognises it. He pays property tax to the county and calls these payments tributes, to keep relations friendly.
zaqistan.mechanism: Owning land and paying local tax on it causes no conflict with the state, so the state has no reason to act. The land stays in Utah under American law.

add_sources.t: Man creates Republic of Zaqistan in Box Elder County (Deseret News)

set.anchor: Northwestern Box Elder County, Utah; exact site is withheld, position estimated

zaqistan.why: Site narrowed to northwestern Box Elder County, so the point was moved from the center of Utah (estimated). Founder is Zaq Landsberg (founder field says Not stated).
